---
title: "Trade-offs"
subtitle: "What was prioritised, what was refused, and the mistakes worth knowing about."
---

## How the work was ordered

Thirteen phases, each with a review gate. The ordering was not by feature value; it was by
**what would invalidate later work if it were wrong**.

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
  P0["0. Foundation"] --> P1["1 and 2. Target system, bundles, splits, leakage controls"]
  P1 --> P2["3 and 4. Tools, graph, triage"]
  P2 --> P3["5 and 6. Eval harness, baselines"]
  P3 --> P4["7 to 10. Critic, gate, cascade, security, self-improvement"]
  P4 --> P5["11 and 12. Console, observability, site"]
  style P1 fill:#fff8e8
  style P3 fill:#fff8e8
```

The two highlighted phases came before any agent existed, and that was the single most
consequential choice in the project.

**Leakage controls before the agent.** If the agent can see the label, every number afterwards
is worthless, and the failure is silent: a leak does not crash, it produces an accuracy figure
that means nothing. So the import-graph walk, the canaries and the split design were built and
tested before there was anything to leak to.

**The harness before the agent.** Building the measuring instrument first means the first thing
you learn about your system is how well it does, rather than how good the demo looks. It is also
why this project can say it has no result: the instrument exists and reports honestly, including
when the answer is "nothing has been measured".

## Decisions and what each one cost

Fourteen decision records, each with the alternatives it rejected. The ones where the cost is
most visible:

| Decision | Rejected | What it cost |
|---|---|---|
| Typed tool templates | Free-form queries | The agent can only ask the fourteen questions somebody wrote a tool for |
| Deterministic triage first | Letting the model explore | A fault the statistics miss is one the agent never sees |
| Frozen bundles for replay | Live-only evaluation | Recording the library is ~36 hours of wall clock and cannot be compressed |
| Approval service as sole writer | Firebreak executing its own fixes | Nothing is ever fixed automatically, by construction |
| Gate removes claims | Annotating them | A report can come back thinner than the investigation was |
| Spans carry shapes, never content | Shipping prompts for debugging | Debugging a bad prompt from a trace is not possible |
| Two telemetry pipelines | One with a distinguishing attribute | More to deploy, and the simpler option fails silently |

## Things that were measured and then refused

This is the section worth reading, because refusing a change that looks good is harder than
making one.

::: {.callout-warning}
## A threshold retune that would have doubled sensitivity

On the recordings available, lowering the abstention threshold from 22.7 to about 13.4 would
more than double sensitivity at **no measured cost** in specificity.

It was not done, for three reasons:

1. **There is one no-fault recording.** Fitting a threshold whose entire job is specificity to a
   single negative example is fitting noise.
2. **Three of the positives sit exactly at the score cap.** The gap a midpoint would sit in is
   as much an artefact of clipping as a property of the data.
3. **It would not fix the real problem.** The two faults that would still be missed are latency
   faults scoring *below* the healthy recording. No threshold on a top anomaly score can catch a
   latency fault without crying wolf on a busy healthy system. That needs a second signal, not a
   better number.

The shipped value is the fixture-tuned one and is labelled as such everywhere it appears.
:::

::: {.callout-warning}
## Published techniques that measured worse

The ranking's parameters were each chosen by ablation, and two well-known improvements were
measured as regressions here:

| Mechanism | Published as | Measured, top-1 of 147 |
|---|---|---|
| Endpoint scaling | An improvement | 147 with, 143 without. **Kept** |
| Self-loops | An improvement | 143 with, 147 without. **Dropped** |
| Backward edges | An improvement | 10 with, 147 without. **Dropped** |

Backward edges are the interesting one: they feed score back into the upstream symptoms the
ranking exists to demote, so they actively undo the mechanism. Adopting all three because they
are published would have produced a system that ranks almost at random.
:::

## Mistakes worth knowing about

Every one of these was found, and most were found by something other than a test.

| What happened | How it was found | What changed |
|---|---|---|
| Six of fourteen recordings silently corrupted by a laptop sleeping mid-run | A bundle looked complete with a hole in the middle | Duration and continuity checks; the recorder refuses such a bundle |
| `make console` broken for an entire phase while 34 tests said the Console worked | Somebody typed the command | Tests that resolve the documented interface, not just the code behind it |
| Eval reports ordered by modification time, which git rewrites on checkout | Two reports shared a checkout timestamp | Ordered by the report's own `generated_at`. A branch switch could have promoted a fixture run reporting perfect accuracy |
| The coverage floor was 84.5%, not the 85% twelve reports named | A run printed FAIL and exited 0 | `precision = 2`, so the message and the exit code agree |
| A config file carried a key nothing read, whose comment described control flow the code does not have | An audit of all 80 models | `extra="forbid"`, and the vocabulary declared once |
| Four separate defects in the tool that reports whether CI passed | Using it | Tests for it, and it now answers for every workflow |

::: {.callout-note}
## The pattern in all of them

Two components agreeing on a type and disagreeing on a vocabulary, failing silently. It came up
**nine times**. The remedy each time was the same: declare the vocabulary once, and assert it in
a contract test.

The second pattern: **the thing that tells you whether everything else is fine is the thing
nobody checks.** Four of the nine were in the CI status tool, the hygiene checks, or the
conformance checker.
:::

## What was deliberately not built

Recorded as decisions with reasons, not as omissions:

- **A collector config and Grafana dashboards.** Nothing here runs a collector. Shipping
  untested config that looks like a working observability stack is worse than a recorded gap.
- **Live streaming of an investigation.** Against a frozen bundle a run finishes in under a
  second, so a progress bar would be theatre.
- **Charting libraries.** There is one graph worth drawing and no calibration curve with enough
  data to plot.
- **An approve button in the Console.** It would put the decision and the credential back in one
  process, which is the arrangement the whole design avoids.
